The Nene (Branta sandvicensis) displays a life history shaped by the resource-limited environment of the Hawaiian Islands. Females typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], laying up to four eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = up to four eggs per nesting attempt], a modest reproductive output that reflects the low productivity of their volcanic habitats. Newly laid eggs have an initial wet weight of approximately 131 grams [Ww0 = approximately 131 grams], a substantial mass that supports a well-developed embryo during the protracted incubation period. In captive breeding programs where eggs are artificially incubated at a constant temperature of 36 °C, hatching occurs after about 30 days [ab = about 30 days] at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration comparable to that of other large-bodied waterfowl. At the moment of hatching, the wet weight of the neonate is recorded as 90.8 grams [Wwb = 90.8 grams], representing a small but critical reduction from the initial egg mass due to metabolic consumption and water loss during development.

The developmental trajectory of the gosling is carefully timed to coincide with seasonal resource pulses. Fledging, defined as the achievement of independent flight, occurs approximately 63 days after hatching [tx = approximately 63 days after hatching], a relatively long period for a goose species that reflects the need for extensive feather development and muscular strengthening in a predator-free but nutritionally dilute environment. Following this milestone, juveniles enter a prolonged phase of somatic growth and social learning. Sexual maturity, as indicated by the onset of gonadal activity and the development of adult plumage, is not reached until about 189 days after hatching [tp = about 189 days after hatching], a relatively late maturation compared to continental waterfowl. This means that young birds typically delay their first reproductive effort until the following breeding season, even though they are physiologically capable of breeding before the end of their first calendar year of life.

Adult body size in the Nene exhibits a subtle but consistent sexual dimorphism. Field measurements from long-term monitoring studies on the island of Hawai'i indicate that adult females attain a maximum body mass of around 1930 grams [Wwi = around 1930 grams], while males, which are structurally larger, reach an ultimate body mass of approximately 2010 grams [Wwi = approximately 2010 grams]. This modest weight difference of roughly 4 percent is less pronounced than in many continental goose species, possibly due to the reduced selective pressure for male-male competition in low-density island populations. The overall body mass of adults is considerably lower than that of the closely related Canada goose, an adaptation that may reduce energetic demands during the non-breeding season when food resources are scarce. These mass values represent asymptotic measurements from repeatedly sampled individuals that had completed their primary growth phase, as confirmed by growth curve analysis of captive-reared birds.

Reproductive timing in the Nene is highly variable across the archipelago, primarily driven by local rainfall patterns that govern the availability of tender grass shoots and fern fronds. On the island of Kaua'i, where year-round precipitation is more reliable, the time since birth at first brood is approximately 2 years [tR = approximately 2 years], allowing females to breed in their second calendar year. In contrast, the more seasonal environment of Mauna Loa's slopes on the Big Island imposes a longer developmental delay, with the time since birth at first brood extending to roughly 3 years [tR = roughly 3 years]. This variation likely reflects differences in the rate at which juveniles can accumulate sufficient body condition to meet the energetic demands of egg production and incubation. The two-year delay observed in favorable habitats is among the shortest recorded for any goose species, while the three-year delay aligns with the life history patterns of other island-endemic waterfowl. The daily reproduction rate can be expressed as 0.011 offspring per day [Ri = 0.011 offspring per day], consistent with the low fecundity typical of this species.

Longevity records for the Nene indicate a maximum lifespan in the wild of approximately 15,330 days [am = approximately 15,330 days], an exceptional duration for a bird of this body size and one that places it among the longest-lived of all Anseriformes. This extreme longevity is a classic correlate of a "slow" life history, characterized by low annual fecundity and delayed reproduction, which together buffer populations against the high variance in juvenile survival typical of stochastic island environments. Individuals that survive past the vulnerable first few years can continue breeding for several decades, given that there is no evidence of reproductive senescence until very late in life. The combination of a high annual adult survival rate, a maximum longevity exceeding four decades, and a clutch size of just four eggs per year underscores the conservative reproductive strategy that has allowed this species to persist despite habitat loss and introduced predators.
